newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium airlifts troops for Zaire evacution.
newsitem.headline: Belgium airlifts troops for Zaire evacution.

text.p: Belgium started airlifting paratroopers to Zaire on Monday, ready to evacuate Belgian citizens from its war-racked former colony.

Operation "Green Stream", the sixth of its kind since Zairean independence in 1960, will fly 550 Belgian soldiers to Brazzaville, the capital of Congo, which lies just across the Zaire river from the Zairean capital Kinshasa.

"If necessary we'll stay in Brazzaville but I would prefer to get access to Kinshasa to help our nationals," Belgian Defence Minister Jean-Pol Poncelet told BRTN television. "The Americans and French have the same problem," he said.
Tension is running high in the Zairean capital after rebels led by Laurent Kabila overran a fifth of the country in their effort to topple President Mobutu Sese Seko.
In Brazzaville, the Belgians will join 650 U.S. and 40 French soldiers who are also ready to evacuate their nationals, an army spokseman told Reuters.
There are 3,000 Belgians in Zaire, including 1,150 in Kinshasa. The total number of Westerners in the sprawling central African country is estimated at 7,000.
Poncelet told the Belga news agency the mission could last more than a month. An army official said the soldiers could stay longer. "To my knowledge, no deadline has been set," he said.

By 1600 GMT seven C-130 Hercules transport aircraft had left the Melsbroek airbase close to Brussels, carrying equipment. Two army Boeing 727s and a chartered Boeing 767 aircraft were airlifting the troops to Brazzaville after dusk.
Belgian King Albert urged troops to stay calm during their mission.
"Don't be too nervous when nothing happens," he said.
The Belgian government has stressed that the mission is purely humanitarian.
"Our ambition is to help our citizens who want to leave the country. This has no political bearing whatsoever, particularly with regard to the current regime there," Poncelet said Sunday.
People can still leave the country on commercial flights, but many are reluctant to go because they want to protect their business interests.
Since the evacuation was announced on Saturday, about 500 Belgians have returned on commercial flights, a spokesman for Belgian carrier Sabena said.

Since Zaire, formerly the Belgian Congo, won independence in 1960, Belgium has repeatedly sent troops to evacuate nationals during the many crises of Mobutu's reign, most recently in 1991 and 1993, when Kinshasa was overrun by rioting.
In 1978, dozens of Europeans were killed in the Kolwezi mining centre in Shaba province, before Belgian and French paratroopers could move in to evacuate their citizens.
There was also military intervention in 1964, when about a hundred Europeans were killed in a rebellion in the eastern part of the country.
